Schedules and tags are submitted to the CISO and counterparties, with hourly calls where required.
Traders check out with major marketers and utilities each night.
Errors in the schedule sheets, tags or CISO entries are found and corrected.

A requested task was put off to another day for lack of time.

synthesis.description: Volume management and allocation staff spot gas that flowed at a meter with no deal, no nomination or unexpected volumes, sometimes months after the flow. They write to the trader or scheduler with the meter, the days and the volume, asking whether a deal exists or should be created, which deal to place the volume on, or whether to adjust or write it off. Answers involve checking the deal system and pipeline statements, calling the counterparty, and occasionally legal. Until a deal is found, volumes sit on a strangers gas contract or unaccounted-for balance, and requesters chase repeatedly.

Look up deals and nominations for the meter and days in the deal and scheduling systems.
Ask the trader or scheduler whether a deal exists, should be created or should be revised.
Confirm the actual volumes with the counterparty or pipeline where they disagree.
Create, extend or path a deal, or decide to adjust or write off the volume.
Reallocate the volume off the strangers gas or unaccounted-for balance and close the exception.

stalls.summary: Requesters wait on replies and chase repeatedly for status on a meter, sometimes after voicemails, and one escalates in capitals asking for anyone to help resolve the matter.
Resolution depends on outside parties: a scheduler waits for a counterparty contact to call back after speaking with legal before proceeding.
Questions get passed between people without a clear owner: an issue is placed in another person's lap, and requests are redirected to whoever handles or allocates the point.
The same deal and volume questions go round and round between groups without being settled.
System problems create or hide exceptions: mirrored meters misbehave, nothing comes through in the scheduling system, and a change to system defaults is proposed.
Old flow is raised long after the gas moved, with volumes booked to a strangers gas contract while an earlier request for a deal went unanswered.

contradictions.summary: Different people are named as the one who handles meter flow questions: one sender says a named colleague handles it, another says a different person allocates the point, another names the volume management contact, and another says to talk to the desk lead.
Logistics claims it will inform the assets group of meter changes, while volume management staff separately take responsibility for adjustments, so the duty to communicate and correct is split.
The deal system and the pipeline disagree on volumes: discrepancies with the pipeline are listed by day, and a counterparty agrees volumes should have gone elsewhere than recorded.

automation.approach: A daily exception report that matches measured meter flow against deals and nominations and lists each meter, day and volume with no deal, with the last deal at that meter and its trader attached. A routing table names the owner for each meter or point, and a standard request message carries the meter, days, volume and proposed action, with ageing so old items surface before they go stale.
automation.rationale: Requests are written by hand in the same shape again and again: meter, dates, volume, last deal, question. A request form or tracker layout with those fields and a named owner per point cuts lookup and rewriting, and the ageing column addresses the chasing and handoff confusion the mail shows. Deciding how to book the flow stays with people.

Matching and variance listing are repeatable; the judgement on the right price stays with people.

synthesis.description: Settlements and accounting staff find a mismatch between a counterparty invoice or payment and the deal as booked in Sitara: a different price, an unpriced or wrong index, unactualized volumes, a deal that should be netted, or an invoice for gas never paid. They ask the scheduler or trader to verify the deal, correct the ticket or say what to bill, sometimes pulling trader tape recordings or checking published market prices for power disputes. Once the deal is corrected, the invoice is paid or rebilled before the payment date.

They email the scheduler or trader with the deal number and the two figures.
The trader or scheduler checks the deal terms, volumes or published price, sometimes pulling tapes.
The ticket is corrected in Sitara or the counterparty is told the correct price.
Settlements reruns the invoice or payment and confirms before the due date.
Unresolved items are chased or escalated to the counterparty.

stalls.summary: Settlements waits on the scheduler or trader to verify deals, chasing with follow-ups while payment dates approach.
Counterparties do not return calls about outstanding payments or disputed deals.
Confusion over who handles a deal: requests go to the wrong desk or person and are redirected.
Sitara itself blocks fixes: a ticket could not be opened to correct swing pricing, and the system held two prices for one day.
Volumes not yet actualized leave nothing in volume management to settle against.
Staff departures leave items open, with a handler trying to finish what they can before leaving.

contradictions.summary: Invoice and system prices disagree for the same deal: a counterparty billed one price while Sitara showed another, and Sitara held two prices for the same day.
A price change believed final was not the final price for the deal, and a counterparty changed its price mid-dispute.

Ownership of disputed deals is stated differently: one sender was told another person handled the deal, another says a deal belongs to a different desk, and a third asks that all monetized questions go through one person.
Practice conflicts on contacting customers: staff emailed counterparties about disputes while a manager told them not to send dispute emails to customers.

automation.approach: Run a daily match of counterparty invoices against Sitara deal prices and volumes, listing each variance with deal number, both figures, the responsible desk and the payment due date, and send it to the owning scheduler or trader with a standard query. Track each variance to closure so follow-ups and escalations come from the list rather than ad hoc chasing.
automation.rationale: Most rounds are the same question asked in different words: this invoice says one price, Sitara says another, which is right. A standard variance query with the deal number, both figures, due date and owner cuts the clarification loops and misrouting, and a matching report finds the mismatches before they become payment-day emergencies.

automation.rationale: Requests arrive as ad hoc lists in many formats and are repeatedly followed by stragglers; a single layout and an automated match against the master termination list cut rework and make reconciliation straightforward.

Work out average deliveries and utilization against capacity.

synthesis.description: Customers, suppliers and internal desks send daily and monthly gas nominations: Calpine and Enron Methanol send standing daily nomination documents, a pipeline system sends its nomination, and plant and producer contacts send revised volumes when production drops or demand changes. Schedulers and logistics staff enter the volumes in Sitara and on the pipeline, set up the month's estimates, rework deal tickets and meters when a party revises its request, and confirm the change back.
steps: A customer, supplier or desk sends a daily or monthly nomination, or an estimate for the coming month.
The scheduler checks the volumes against the deal, meter and transport contract.
The scheduler enters or updates the volumes in Sitara and nominates them on the pipeline.
When a party revises its volumes, the scheduler updates the setup, deal ticket or meter, sometimes retroactively.
Missing transport numbers or contract details are chased with the counterparty or other desks.
The scheduler confirms the nomination is entered, tracked and balanced.

stalls.summary: Entries are reworked after mistakes or wrong files: a nomination set up wrongly at the start of the month, a spreadsheet sent empty, and a protected deal ticket that blocks correction.
Nominations wait on other parties: a transport number from another desk, and a returned phone call before a change can be confirmed; volumes sit on a temporary contract until new transport is set up.

Systems get in the way: an attachment keeps bouncing off the mail gateway, an online nomination system withdraws temporary passwords, and a counterparty asks which pipelines still accept dial-up nominations.
The same monthly setup is revised again and again within the month as volumes change, each revision re-entered by hand.

Update the customer's month-to-date spreadsheet and send it to the desk.
Receive the customer's or pipeline's actuals, swing volumes or best-available figures.

The distributor checks the report arrived and is the right date.
The report is forwarded to the standing recipient list.
Recipients review exposure and raise questions on missing positions or how figures are derived.

Questions about pricing, documentation from the counterparty and whether a buyback exists at all go back and forth until the supply and market deals are attached as a buy/sell and the month's activity is reviewed.

Confirm the deal terms, pricing type and counterparty documentation.
Create or change the path in the scheduling system for the meter and volume.
Attach the supply deal to the market deal to establish the buy/sell or buyback link.
Circulate the monthly path list for others to check for anything out of line.
Review the month's allocations, links and buybacks and correct what is wrong.

Staff pull measured versus scheduled volumes and prepare a spreadsheet or imbalance report by contract.
The report or a list of meters and contracts goes to the counterparty or pipeline to verify, add or update.
Both sides compare their numbers and request statements to support any volume differences by month.
The parties agree how to clear the imbalance: lend or park gas, adjust nominations, or pay back volumes.

A written procedure that fixes ownership, sign-off and the manual-entry path addresses the stalls directly, while the comparison report takes over the volume pulling.

steps: HR announces the performance cycle and its schedule.
Managers ask staff to pick reviewers, entered in the PEP system or sent by email.
Staff submit their accomplishments and reviewers write feedback.
The manager schedules and holds the PRC meeting to rank staff.
The manager writes each review on the standard form and discusses it with the employee.
Signed copies are collected and filed.

stalls.summary: The PEP system had problems, so reviewer lists had to be sent by email to the manager instead.
Accomplishments and reviews arrived late or needed chasing, including a manager asking for word on a pending review.

automation.rationale: The rounds repeat the same sequence and the stalls are late or misformatted submissions and a fallback when the system failed. A checklist with a standard form makes each stage and its owner clear; the writing and ranking remain people's work.

Counterparties agree how volumes are handled, such as holding gas and batching it later.

automation.rationale: Most rounds are the same announcement re-sent with a new meter list and dates; a standard notice with the meter list drawn from the system cuts the retyping and makes postponements easy to reissue, while staff still agree how volumes are handled.

synthesis.description: Credit and desk leads tell the real-time traders when a counterparty is cut off or cleared to trade again, in short all-desk notices, and the risk side asks for or confirms credit reserves on named transactions. A reserve request is forwarded with the deal details below it, and the reply states how origination was split between the trader and the credit reserve, with any balance taken from the trader's origination that night.

Risk forwards the transaction details and asks for a credit reserve to be taken.
The reserve and origination split is booked and confirmed back to the trader.
Any shortfall in the split is corrected by moving origination from the trader's book.

automation.approach: Keep a single counterparty credit status list that the deal-entry system checks before a trade is booked, and have a reserve request form that captures the deal numbers and the split between trader origination and credit reserve, so the booking and confirmation come from one record instead of free-text email.
automation.rationale: The rounds are short notices and reserve requests; a standard notice and reserve-request message with fixed fields (counterparty, status, effective time, deal numbers, reserve amount, split) would remove ambiguity and the rework seen when a split is corrected afterwards.

steps: A colleague or customer emails asking for index, point or historical price data for given periods.
The recipient checks which source holds the data and whether it has been loaded.

automation.rationale: The requests ask for the same kinds of figures in the same shape. A standard price-data layout lets the person asked fill or forward it quickly, and lets customers see exactly which points and periods are available.

automation.rationale: The requests are short and varied but share the same fields; a standard form removes the back-and-forth over missing people and misrouted roster checks, and gives the requester a status to look at instead of asking.
